claim: Precision Omega reproduces Chroma's published column exactly

baseline.source: Chroma, Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval
baseline.note: the baseline IS the published table; agreement to within 0.05pp is the result

scale: 5 corpora, 328k characters, 472 gold-span questions, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter at four size/overlap settings
code_path: tier-0/model-free + tiktoken cl100k_base for token-sized chunks
surprise: The reading the design record originally assumed -- the minimal set of chunks covering the gold spans, rather than every chunk containing a gold character -- scores 8.6/16.8/17.8/30.7. It is nearly right with no overlap and about 28% high wherever chunks overlap, so it would have passed every unit test written against it and quietly recommended overlap.

claim: Structural signals separate chunking strategies with no questions, no ground truth and no model
baseline: fixed-size splitting, the strategy every pipeline starts with
scale: one 48kB Markdown document; runs in milliseconds on any machine
surprise: Screening disqualifies almost everything on a real document -- code fences cut in half, or sections past the embedding window. That is the honest answer, and it arrives before a pipeline exists.

claim: A strategy can score 100% recall and still be useless, and only an inside-the-chunk metric can say so
baseline: recall alone, which is what chunk-level metrics report
scale: State of the Union transcript, 48k characters, 76 gold-span questions, BM25/FTS5 retriever, k per question
command: uv run chunking-lab score --corpus state_of_the_union.md --strategy structural --strategy recursive:200
surprise: The transcript has no Markdown headings, so the structural splitter emits one chunk holding the entire document. It retrieves the answer every single time. A chunk-level metric scores that a perfect hit.

claim: Model-free query-free signals predict the measured chunker ranking, but mostly by proxying chunk size; duplication and boundary fidelity survive controlling for it
baseline: the raw correlation, which for median_length is close to a tautology because Precision Omega divides by the chunks holding the answer
scale: 14 strategies x 5 corpora x 472 gold-span questions = 70 (corpus, strategy) points, 6608 result rows, ~100s
surprise: Controlling for chunk size was expected to shrink everything; it doubled boundary_fidelity, from ~+0.15 raw to +0.44. Size was masking it, because strategies that cut cleanly also cut larger. Separately, mid_table_rate and split_fence_rate are constant on all five corpora -- the benchmark has no tables or code fences -- so they are untested here rather than disproven, and printing them as 0.00 would have laundered missing data into a result.

claim: mid_table_rate does not predict retrieval quality on any target; split_fence_rate does so only where code is dense; duplication and boundary_fidelity replicate from the prose corpus
baseline: F8, where both structural signals were constant on the Chroma corpora and therefore untested
scale: generated documentation corpus: 5 documents, 180 questions, 14 strategies, 2520 result rows; gold spans known by construction
surprise: mid_table_rate fails for a structural reason rather than a statistical one: cutting through a table row makes the chunks holding the answer smaller, which RAISES Precision Omega. A ceiling metric cannot see table damage even in principle -- the damage is to whether a retrieved chunk is usable. The null result is about the (signal, metric) pair, not the signal.
limitation: The corpus is synthetic. The generator controls where tables and answers are; it does not control whether shredding them hurts, which is measured. External validity is to documentation shaped like this, not to how often such documents occur.

claim: Chunking matters consistently; retrieval matters rarely and then enormously. Their maxima are nearly identical; their frequencies are not.
unit: ratio of best to worst IoU, each axis measured with the other held fixed
baseline: the median-only summary, which said 'the chunker matters more' and hid that the two axes have nearly identical maxima
scale: 5 strategies x 3 retrievers x 5 corpora x 180 questions = 2700 result rows; encoder ollama/nomic-embed-text (768-dim, local); 21 seconds
code_path: vector and hybrid via provider/ollama/nomic-embed-text; bm25 model-free
surprise: All four cases where the retriever mattered are BM25 collapsing and a semantic retriever rescuing it -- 1.3 IoU against 19.7 in the worst. And the tidy explanation, that the retriever matters more when chunking is worse, is false: the rank correlation between a configuration's IoU and its retriever spread is -0.04.
limitation: Five strategies and three retrievers, so a spread is only as wide as the options offered. Synthetic corpus, one encoder, and the comparison must run on IoU because Precision Omega is retriever-independent and would report no retriever effect at all.

claim: Quote-then-locate turns a weak model into less ground truth rather than wrong ground truth; yield depends on the document as much as the model
unit: fraction of attempted questions that were verifiable
baseline: asking the model for character offsets directly, whose failures are invisible rather than countable
scale: 4 real documents from this repo, 5 attempts each, ollama/llama3.1 (local, 8B), seed 42
code_path: provider/ollama/llama3.1 for generation; locating is model-free
surprise: Yield is a property of the (model, corpus) pair. Dense markdown -- tables, code fences, nested lists -- yields about half what prose does, because copying a table row verbatim has far more to get exactly right than copying a sentence. What did not change: every failure was discarded rather than written in with plausible wrong offsets.
superseded: An earlier version of this card reported 25% from 8 attempts over 2 documents. n=8 is too small to state a rate; the larger run gives 70%.
